questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to learn Spanish and since the only other option was Barcelona who mainly speak Catalan, I ended up choosing Granada.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It's not always easy to find the information you need and you're also constantly receiving a lot of information. For any people going I recommend keeping a note/document where you write down everything you're told so you don't have to search for it. All the pdf's, all the codes and websites etc. this was so helpful to me during the first weeks.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had two welcome meetings, one for the whole university and one for the faculty. The exchange office at Granada were also pretty good about replying to any questions you had on whatsapp which was great.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The University doesn't have campus housing, so all of the exchange students have to rent. I rented my studio off AirBnb, which was unusual and meant I paid a little bit extra, I didn't mind spending a bit more money (in comparison to Copenhagen it was still pretty cheap), but I know housing in Granada is generally super affordable if you have roommates.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I encountered no issues about living off campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I don't know if I can be satisfied with the housing available when the University didn't offer housing? I was happy with the apartment I rented

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Again, there is a lot of documents, and Granada is still a University that requires more paperwork and doesn't have the electronic process for some of the application. This wasn't a huge deal and I found the exchange office to be quite helpful and usually pretty quick at replying.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The part that was most difficult was finding courses that could be equivalent to the courses I had back home, the application itself and the different types of documents to upload I actually found pretty easy to do in Mobility Online.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could ask questions at the welcome meetings, and could email and text the exchange office, I also found that the exchange students were good at helping one another

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: To keep all the documents you're asked to provide in one place so they can easily be found and also to ask if you're unsure.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I don't think I can entirely blame the University of Granada for my dissatisfaction with the academic level, I had been warned before coming to Spain that the classes would not be to the same level as the ones in Copenhagen. 
My main issue was actually that I felt the students were never given enough information about what was expected of them, usually we didn't know about assignments or papers due before the week they were due, and this stressed me out so much. I felt like I was perpetually behind and could never catch up. Again, this isn't really the fault of the University rather it's just my personality, but it made my exchange very stressful at times.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The reports I read stressed that the level was a lot lower than the classes in Copenhagen, I would agree with this partially. Rather, I found that UGR uses a completely different type of learning then we're used to. Essentially, all of the classes are just about remembering information and being able to recite this information, there is very little discussion or debate if any, and you're rarely asked to analyze or compare which is what I'm used to.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is clearly a more traditional learning environment, where what the teacher says, is what is correct and there is a lot less room for debate. Depending on the teacher I also experienced some getting slightly upset if I asked critical questions, however this isn't applicable to everyone and generally speaking I thought most of the teachers were nice enough.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
International Organizations
Theory of Democracy: Gender and Interculturality
Sistemas Políticos de Países Emergentes (Political Systems of Emerging Countries) 
Politica Comparada (Comparative Politics) 
Sistemas Políticos y Jurídicos de la UE (Political and Judicial Systems of the EU) 

With these classes Comparative Politics + Political Systems of Emerging Countries = DAK3
Political and Judicial Systems of the EU + International Organizations = EP 
And Theory of Democracy was an elective course

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I'll be honest I don't have a specific class that I thought was very good. Instead, my recommendation would be to take some classes in Spanish if your goal is to learn Spanish. I had a lot of friends who only had classes in English, and then just didn't learn a lot of Spanish because it's hard to make friends with locals. While the Spanish classes are obviously harder, it also felt like a different way to get something out of the teaching, since the level is generally low.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None really, it's cheap to live in Spain and I didn't have to buy any books for my classes.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Everything was less expensive than I expected, especially groceries you could get by really cheaply. Also if you go to the cafeteria at the University, you pay like 30DKK and get a very substantial meal, which I would often do and it saved me a lot of money.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't partake in any clubs or sports.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I know they had different sports activities and did movie showings etc. they go through them at the welcome meeting

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I wouldn't know.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Granada is a very cozy town and I know a lot of exchange students also visit a lot of cities nearby like Cordoba, Sevilla, Malaga and also go to Sierra Nevada to hike or down to the beach. Generally, I found Granada to be a really nice place to live, even if it might be a bit boring to be a tourist in.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Obviously it's harder to adjust when you're also trying to learn a new language, but I think I found it pretty easy to adjust to the local culture

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Genuinely, just start a conversation, this is another reason I was happy to have classes in Spanish. The exchange students are usually pretty bad about only hanging out with other exchange students, but because I was in classes where I was one of very few international students, it made it a lot easier to talk to the spanish students. In my experience the local students were so welcoming and eager to invite you to things if you just said hi.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It was very weird to have classes in the evening, my classes from 8-10pm specifically was hard to get used to. I think the hardest thing was the language part, mainly just forcing yourself into situations where you'll be speaking Spanish.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love how extroverted the Spanish people I became friends with were, and how easy they made it to be a part of their group even though my Spanish was terrible. So the people would absolutely have to be number 1, but the tapas culture if also amazing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. That it is a very different type of learning which can feel very frustrating at times
2. If your goal is to learn Spanish, in my experience, you have to do more to achieve that then just be in Spain
3. Making local friends is not actually as difficult as it feels and really made my exchange

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not really, but I remember that it can feel like such a chaotic experience to go through the process of registering and picking classes etc. So if you have any questions about what I've written in this evaluation or just questions in general you can text me on messenger, my name is Viktoria Ringsmose.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To learn a new language and to make some great friends

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To learn a new language and to get used to the different learning environment

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
